name: Tubular / long corolla
simpleBlurb: A deep tube puts nectar out of reach for short-tongued visitors and favors birds or long-tongued moths.
shapeSummary: Elongated corolla tube with nectar at the base and often a narrow opening.
fruitSet: When the right long-tongued visitor threads the tube, pollen is placed precisely on the body and later stigmas. Mismatch with short-tongued insects often means visits without pollen transfer, so fruit set stays low even when flowers look busy.

name: Open bowl / dish
simpleBlurb: A wide, shallow flower invites many insects to land and walk across pollen-rich centers.
shapeSummary: Broad, open corolla with exposed reproductive parts and easy landing space.
fruitSet: Generalist insect traffic can deliver plenty of pollen, which supports fruit set in self-incompatible crops when bloom overlaps with active foragers. Incomplete visits or rainy weather that grounds bees quickly cut seed and fruit numbers.

name: Brush / bottlebrush
simpleBlurb: A spray of stamens presents pollen like a brush that wipes onto fur, feathers, or large insects.
shapeSummary: Reduced petals with a dense brush of protruding stamens and accessible nectar.
fruitSet: Brush blossoms transfer pollen mechanically as a visitor brushes through. Fruit set tracks how often capable visitors arrive during the receptive window; in some regions vertebrate pollinators dominate this form.

name: Lip / orchid-like
simpleBlurb: A landing lip and bilateral shape steer a specialist insect into a precise pollen path.
shapeSummary: Strong bilateral symmetry with a labellum (lip) that orients the visitor.
fruitSet: Many orchids package pollen as pollinia, so one correct visit can fertilize thousands of ovules—or none if the wrong insect fails to pick up or deposit pollinia. Fruit set is often pollinator-limited rather than resource-limited.

name: Composite head
simpleBlurb: What looks like one flower is many florets on a shared disc, feeding bees and butterflies efficiently.
shapeSummary: Capitulum of ray and/or disc florets sharing a flat or convex landing surface.

traits.corollaDepth: short florets on a shared head

fruitSet: Each floret can set an independent achene. Dense bee activity across the head raises seed set; sparse pollination leaves a hollow center of empty seeds even when the head looks intact.

name: Gullet / personate
simpleBlurb: The mouth stays closed until a heavy bee pushes in, so light visitors rarely steal nectar without moving pollen.
shapeSummary: Bilabiate flower with a closed throat that requires force to open.
fruitSet: Only visitors strong enough to pry the gullet open contact anthers and stigma in sequence. Without those bees, flowers may be visited by thieves around the side and fruit set collapses.

name: Bell / campanulate
simpleBlurb: A hanging or upright bell shelters nectar and often suits bees that can hang or crawl inside.
shapeSummary: Campanulate corolla forming a protected chamber.
fruitSet: Bumble bees that sonicate or crawl into bells move pollen effectively among plants. Cool springs that delay bee flight during peak bloom are a classic cause of poor fruit set in bell-flowered orchard relatives and ornamentals.

name: Trap / carrion cue
simpleBlurb: Heat, odor, and a chamber lure flies that normally seek carrion; this is an educational extreme, not a garden default.
shapeSummary: Chambered or pitfall-like flower with strong odor and often mottled color.
fruitSet: Fruit set depends on temporarily trapping and releasing flies that carry pollen between plants. Without the right fly fauna, these specialists set little fruit despite dramatic blooms.

name: Wind-pollinated
simpleBlurb: Petals shrink or vanish; clouds of light pollen ride air currents instead of animal bodies.
shapeSummary: Reduced perianth, dangling anthers, feathery stigmas, no showy nectar guides.
fruitSet: Fruit and seed set track weather and plant density more than insect flights. Still air, rain during pollen shed, or isolated plantings can leave ovaries unfertilized even though no pollinator was ever required.

name: Closed / cleistogamous
simpleBlurb: Some flowers never open and fertilize themselves, producing fruit without a pollinator visit.
shapeSummary: Bud-like closed flowers that self-pollinate; often alongside showy open flowers on the same plant.
fruitSet: Cleistogamous flowers guarantee some seed set without insects, which is insurance when pollinators are scarce. They do not replace outcrossing benefits of open flowers when genetic mixing matters for disease resistance or yield quality.

name: Spurred
simpleBlurb: A nectar spur filters visitors by tongue length, matching bees, butterflies, or moths to a precise fit.
shapeSummary: Corolla with a hollow spur holding nectar beyond a short tongue’s reach.
fruitSet: Spur–tongue matching raises legitimate pollen transfer. Nectar robbers that pierce the spur can leave flowers emptied and fruit set depressed even when visits look frequent.

name: Urn / urceolate
simpleBlurb: A constricted mouth on a swollen corolla favors bees that hang and buzz, classic in blueberries and kin.
shapeSummary: Urn-shaped corolla with a narrow aperture and enclosed anthers.
fruitSet: Buzz-pollinating bees shake pollen from poricidal anthers. Commercial blueberry fruit set rises when mason bees or bumble bees are active at bloom; honey bees alone are sometimes less effective on urn flowers.
